title: Irregular spotting on the injection
answer: In the first months of using the injection, many people have spotting or bleeding at unexpected times. This is common and not harmful. Over time, bleeding often becomes less, and many users stop bleeding completely. It does not mean the injection is not working. If the spotting bothers you, talk to a health worker; they may be able to help, and you can decide together whether to continue.

title: No periods on the injection
answer: Many people who use the injection stop having periods, especially after a year of use. This is expected and safe. The blood is not collecting inside your body or making you sick; the lining of the womb just stays thin because of the hormone. Periods usually return some months after stopping the injection. If you have signs of pregnancy or are worried, visit a health center for a check.

title: Heavy bleeding on the injection
answer: Heavy or long bleeding is uncommon with the injection, but it can happen, usually in the first months. If you bleed much more than your normal period, for more than 8 days, or feel weak or dizzy, go to your health center. A health worker can check for other causes and may offer treatment. If you soak pads very quickly, faint or feel very unwell, go to a health facility now or call 112.

title: Delay in fertility after stopping the injection
answer: After stopping DMPA, it usually takes longer to get pregnant than with other methods. On average it takes several months longer, and for some people up to about a year after the last injection. This delay is temporary. The injection does not cause permanent infertility. If you plan a pregnancy soon, you may prefer a method with faster return. If you are not pregnant after a year of trying, see a health worker.

title: Waiting for periods to return after the injection
answer: After your last DMPA injection, it can take several months for your periods to come back. At first they may be irregular. This is normal and not harmful; your body is adjusting as the hormone wears off. If you have not had a period by about a year after your last injection, or you think you might be pregnant, visit a health center for a check.

answer: If you get your first injection within 7 days after your period starts, it protects you right away. If you get it at another time, use condoms or avoid sex for the next 7 days. title: How effective the injection is
answer: The injection is very effective when you get each injection on time. With typical use, about 4 in 100 users get pregnant in a year, mostly because they are late for an injection. When injections are always on time, fewer than 1 in 100 get pregnant. Keep your appointment dates. The injection does not protect against STIs or HIV, so use condoms if there is any risk.

If you do not want to get pregnant, start another method before your next injection would have been due.

title: How the copper IUD prevents pregnancy
answer: The copper IUD is a small, flexible T-shaped device placed inside the womb by a trained provider. The copper changes the way sperm move so they cannot reach and fertilise an egg. It has no hormones, so it does not change your natural cycle, though periods may become heavier. It works for many years and can be removed whenever you want.

title: How long a copper IUD lasts
answer: A copper IUD can protect you from pregnancy for up to 12 years. You do not need to keep it that long; you can have it removed whenever you want, for any reason. Your provider will write the date on your card. When it expires, it can be removed and replaced with a new one at the same visit if you wish.

title: What the hormonal IUD is
answer: The hormonal IUD is a small T-shaped device placed in the womb that slowly releases a progestin hormone. It thickens cervical mucus so sperm cannot pass. It works for several years, often 3 to 8 depending on the type. Periods usually become lighter, and some users stop bleeding. It may not be available at every facility, so ask your health worker if they offer it.

title: Copper IUD vs hormonal IUD
answer: Both are placed in the womb and are very effective. The copper IUD has no hormones and lasts up to 12 years, but may make periods heavier or more painful, especially at first. The hormonal IUD releases a small amount of progestin, lasts several years, and usually makes periods lighter, sometimes stopping them. Neither protects against STIs. A health worker can help you compare them for your needs.

title: What IUD strings are
answer: IUD strings are two thin threads attached to the IUD. They hang through the cervix into the top of the vagina. They are used to check that the IUD is in place and help the provider remove it later. The strings are soft and usually cannot be seen from outside the body. They do not cause infection and should not be pulled.

title: Checking your IUD strings
answer: You can check your strings after each period, especially in the first months. Wash your hands, sit or squat, and gently put a finger into your vagina until you feel the cervix, which feels firm like the tip of your nose. You should feel the soft strings. Do not pull them. If you cannot feel them, they feel longer or shorter, or you feel the hard IUD, see your provider and use condoms meanwhile.

title: IUD and infection: facts
answer: The IUD itself does not cause infection. There is a small risk of pelvic infection in the first few weeks after insertion, mainly if a person already has an STI like gonorrhoea or chlamydia. That is why a provider asks questions and may check for STIs. After that, risk is very low. Using condoms protects against STIs. Fever, belly pain or bad-smelling discharge need a health worker quickly.

title: Rumour: IUD travels through the body
answer: The IUD cannot travel to your heart, brain or other organs. It stays in the womb. Checking your strings and attending follow-up helps make sure it is in place.

answer: A trained provider removes an IUD by gently pulling on the strings with a small instrument. It usually takes only a minute or two. You may feel a short cramp.
